title: How Magnets Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how magnets work, starting with natural loadstone (magnetite) from Magnesia, then the types of magnets (permanent/hard, temporary/soft, electromagnets, ceramic, Alnico, neodymium, samarium-cobalt, magnetic polymers). They cover how magnets are made (stroking, hammering, electric current, strong fields), magnetic domains and hysteresis, demagnetization by heat (Curie point), and the atomic-level role of unpaired electron spin in iron, cobalt and nickel. They discuss measuring magnetic fields (gauss, tesla), uses of magnets (speakers, motors, MRI, maglev, roller coasters, magnetosphere and auroras), pulsed electromagnetic field bone healing, magnet therapy claims, magnetized water, and a listener shout-out to Trevor and Tony. Includes a sponsor break for Jack Threads.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to magnets
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about how much they know about magnets, discuss everyday fridge magnets, and mention loadstone from Magnesia and Alnico speakers.

segments.title: Basic properties and types of magnets
segments.summary: Basic facts: magnets attract ferrous metals, have north and south poles, opposite poles attract. Magnetism is one of the four fundamental forces. Permanent (hard) versus temporary (soft) magnets, and electromagnets, with a doorbell example. Ceramic, Alnico, neodymium and samarium cobalt magnets and magnetic polymers are compared by strength.

segments.title: Toy magnets and tangent
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh talk about magnetic iron-filing toys and a digression on vintage 1940s-60s dolls, including Rushed hobo dolls.

segments.title: Early magnetization and compasses
segments.summary: Discussion of how people first magnetized iron pins by stroking them with loadstone around the twelfth century, leading to the earliest compasses floated in water.

segments.title: Magnetic domains and why magnets attract and repel
segments.summary: Magnetic domains are tiny magnets within ferromagnetic materials. Aligned domains make a strong field; opposite poles attract and like poles repel because field lines flow in opposite directions.

segments.title: Making magnets and hysteresis
segments.summary: Methods of magnetizing material: stroking, hammering while aligned, passing electric current, and natural formation in lava or lightning. Modern production uses strong magnetic fields. Hysteresis is the delay as domains realign; harder-to-align materials stay magnetized longer.

segments.title: Demagnetization
segments.summary: Magnets can be demagnetized by a reverse field or by heating past the Curie point; a video demonstration used a lighter on a paper clip.

segments.title: Shipping large magnets
segments.summary: Tracy Wilson's section on shipping large magnets, which pick up iron from trucks; magnets are often magnetized on site or electromagnets are used.

segments.title: Atomic-level explanation: electron spin
segments.summary: Electrons in atoms pair with opposite spins (Pauli exclusion). Iron, cobalt and nickel have unpaired electrons spinning the same way, creating magnetic moments and domains. Diamagnetic materials repel instead.

segments.title: Measuring magnetism and uses of magnets
segments.summary: Magnetic field strength measured with gauss meters, in gauss and tesla (10,000 gauss per tesla), and oersted. Uses include speakers, cassette tapes, burglar alarms, motors, car speedometers, CRT televisions, maglev trains, roller coaster brakes, MRI, and the magnetosphere producing auroras.

segments.title: Pulsed electromagnetic fields, cows and magnet health claims
segments.summary: Pulsed electromagnetic fields are used to help heal bone, with a possible use in astronaut garments. Cows with hardware disease are given magnets; swallowed magnets are dangerous for humans. Magnetic bracelets and insoles lack proof of benefit; magnetized drinking water and magnetic water softeners also lack clinical support according to Consumer Reports.

segments.title: Listener mail: shout-out for Trevor and Tony
segments.summary: A deployed service member, Trevor, asks for a shout-out to his wife Tony, saying the podcast helps them talk. Hosts mention how to contact the show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and show contact information, with a sponsor credit to Jack Threads.
